notes:
I've written notes for 21 of the 24 verses. I found nothing usable for vv. 13, 14 and 16, so those are left out. I also found no source on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter, no NET Bible or Bible Odyssey notes, and nothing from a Lutheran or Orthodox site. My copy of the Enduring Word commentary stopped at v. 12, so its points on later verses come only from the site's short AI summary of Guzik.

**v. 1**
- Paul says "by the will of God" because the Corinthians thought little of him: no one made him an apostle, so their low view doesn't lower his standing before God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Guzik notes that Paul calls this troubled church "saints," meaning ordinary people set apart by trusting Jesus, not a spiritual elite. Including "all Achaia" shows the letter was meant to be shared round the region. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Matthew Henry says calling Timothy "brother" shows Paul's humility and his wish to raise the young man's standing. He also says that in Christ, city and country believers stand on the same level. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm

**v. 2**
- Henry says grace and peace belong together, because there is no lasting peace without true grace. Both come from the Father and from Christ, who is "prayed to as God." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm
- Guzik says believers are God's children "by adoption" and "by redemption," not by nature as Jesus is God's Son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/

**v. 3**
- The Greek word for comfort, *paraklesis*, means more than sympathy. It carries the sense of strengthening and making brave. Guzik adds that Father, Son and Spirit are each called Comforter in the New Testament. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Henry links "God of all comfort" to the Spirit, the Comforter, and to the Spirit given in v. 22. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm

**v. 4**
- God comforts us partly so we can comfort others. Guzik warns that pride can keep us from receiving the comfort God sends through other people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Chrysostom points out that Paul doesn't say God keeps us out of trouble, but that He comforts us in it, like the three young men in the furnace. The present tense ("comforts") shows God does this constantly. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220201.htm

**v. 5**
- Henry: they are called "the sufferings of Christ" because Christ feels with His people when they suffer for Him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm
- Guzik, quoting Hodge, says this is about suffering for Christ and borne in a Christian way, not suffering as such. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Chrysostom (an early Greek Church Father) finds comfort in sharing Christ's sufferings at all. He takes "abound" to mean the apostles suffered even more than Christ did, and links the verse to Colossians 1:24. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220201.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik says suffering made Paul rely on God and so made him a more useful minister. The word for endurance (*hupomone*) means triumphant persistence, not passive giving in. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Ellicott says "comfort" is the inward side of what Paul describes, and "salvation" is the outward side: real rescue from evil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/1-6.htm
- **Different emphasis:** Chrysostom says salvation comes "not through believing only" but also through enduring suffering, and that salvation consists in suffering evil rather than doing it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220202.htm

**v. 7**
- Henry: if we copy the faith and patience of good people in trouble, we can hope to share their comfort now and their salvation later. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm
- Gill takes the "consolation" to be comfort in this life, a pledge of future joy, rather than heaven itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/1-7.htm
- Chrysostom: Paul gently calls the Corinthians sharers in sufferings they hardly endured, and gives them credit for his comfort. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220202.htm

**v. 8**
- No one knows what the trouble in Asia was. Guzik lists five suggestions: the "wild beasts" at Ephesus, a synagogue flogging, the riot at Ephesus, persecution before Troas, or a recurring illness. He leans, tentatively, towards illness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Henry is also unsure, suggesting the Demetrius riot or the beasts at Ephesus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm

**v. 9**
- God brings His people to the end of themselves so they will trust His all-sufficiency. "Our extremity is God's opportunity." Raising the dead proves He can do anything. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm
- Guzik reads "in ourselves" as an inner sense of impending death, not a court sentence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Chrysostom: the trials were extreme "lest we should be high minded." Each rescue from near death is a picture of the resurrection. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220202.htm

**v. 10**
- Guzik sees God at work in three tenses: He delivered, He delivers, He will deliver. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Henry: past rescues encourage faith, and distrusting God later dishonours what He has already done. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm

**v. 11**
- Trusting God doesn't replace prayer. Even an apostle wanted others' prayers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm
- Guzik: Paul gave praying believers much of the credit for his ministry. The word "persons" literally means "faces," picturing faces lifted in prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
- Chrysostom stresses giving thanks for blessings given to others, since we all gain from one another's virtue. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220202.htm

**v. 12**
- Henry calls conscience "God's deputy in the soul." Paul appeals to it to answer critics who doubted he was an apostle, not to show off. He means the whole pattern of his life, driven by grace rather than worldly scheming. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm

**vv. 15–17**
- Henry: Paul really did mean to come, for the Corinthians' benefit, and his critics seized on the change of plan to discredit him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_001.cfm
- The Enduring Word summary says the change was pastoral restraint, sparing them a second painful visit, not fickleness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/

**vv. 18–19**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Christ's "yea" is faithfulness to His word, the opposite of "yea and nay," which means going back on one's word. https://biblehub.com/m/2_corinthians/1-20.htm
- Piper (Desiring God) notes how Paul ties an ordinary travel question to the deepest truths about Christ. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/every-promise-is-yes-in-him

**v. 20**
- Piper bases the verse on union with Christ: all God's promises are "yes" for those in Him. The believer's "Amen" is a life that says yes to God even in suffering. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/every-promise-is-yes-in-him
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: older manuscripts read "through Him is the Amen." "Yea" is God's word and "Amen" is His oath, so our assurance is doubled. https://biblehub.com/m/2_corinthians/1-20.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): the promises are true in themselves and fulfilled for those who believe. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n84/2-corinthians/1-20.html

**v. 21**
- Ellicott: "in Christ" is literally "into Christ," meaning being joined to Him. "Anointed" points to a definite moment, when believers received the Spirit at baptism or the laying on of hands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/1-21.htm
- Barnes: the first "us" is Paul, the second includes the Corinthians. Paul credits God, not himself, for his reliability. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/1-21.htm
- Bible Hub's study note says the anointing equips all believers for service. https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/1-21.htm
- Constable says it happened when they trusted Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/1-21.html
- The Biblical Illustrator argues it can't mean ordination to office, because it belongs to all Christians. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/1-21.html

**v. 22: the clearest disagreements**
- **Is the seal a sacrament?**
  - *Baptist (Gill):* the seal is the Spirit Himself. It is not baptism or the Lord's Supper, which are never called seals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/1-22.htm
  - *Ellicott (Anglican):* the Spirit, given after baptism or the laying on of hands, seals God's covenant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/1-22.htm
  - *Catholic (Haydock):* the verse refers to the permanent mark given in baptism, confirmation and ordination, which can never be repeated. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/1-21.html
  - *Orthodox:* a Bible Hub Q&A (not an Orthodox site) links chrismation, an anointing with oil, to this seal. https://mail.biblehub.com/q/what's_chrismation's_purpose_in_christianity.htm
- **Can the seal be lost?**
  - Bible Hub's study note says nothing can break it. https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/1-22.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary agrees the seal "cannot... be broken." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/1-22.htm
  - The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary says the seal "may be lost" and the deposit forfeited. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/1-22.html
  - Maclaren ties security to faith and a present likeness to the Spirit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/2corinthians/seal-and-earnest.cfm
- **Conversion or later experience?**
  - Bible Hub's study note calls sealing a decisive act at conversion. https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/1-22.htm
  - Winslow urges believers to seek the sealing. The Biblical Illustrator describes it as a deepening of grace that brings growing assurance. https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_corinthians/1-22.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/1-22.html
- **Reformed (Calvin):** the Spirit seals the certainty of God's word on our hearts. Without that witness, people claim the name Christian "on false grounds." https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol40/htm/vii.v.htm
- **Methodist (Clarke):** the sealing confirmed Paul's calling through miraculous gifts and gives a "clear testimony" of being accepted by God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/1-22.html
- **Deposit (earnest):** a down payment guaranteeing full payment later. Maclaren sees anointing, sealing and deposit as three sides of one gift. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/2corinthians/seal-and-earnest.cfm
- **Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith):** God gives the Spirit to prove He means to finish redeeming us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/1-22.html
- **Enduring Word summary:** anointing empowers for service, sealing marks and protects, and the deposit pledges more to come. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/

**v. 23**
- Guzik cites this verse when discussing oaths: Scripture doesn't forbid every oath, and godly people used them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/
- Constable says Paul backs his explanation with a solemn oath: he stayed away to spare them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/1-22.html

**v. 24**
- The Enduring Word summary says leaders are fellow workers for their people's joy, not rulers over their faith or consciences. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-1/
